mappings.expected_back: At a stop sign, stop at the clearly marked stop line when one is present.
At a stop sign without a stop line, stop before the crosswalk on the near side of the intersection.
At a stop sign with neither a stop line nor a crosswalk, stop before entering the intersecting highway at the nearest point where approaching traffic can be seen.
A Yield sign requires slowing and yielding to vehicles and pedestrians in the intersection being crossed or on the road being entered.
At a Yield sign, stop before crossing the intersection or entering the highway if that is necessary to yield safely.
The eight-sided stop sign requires a complete stop before the stop line or crosswalk.
Where no stop line or crosswalk exists, stop before the intersection at the nearest position providing a safe view of approaching traffic.
At a yield sign, reduce speed and stop when needed to give other traffic the right of way.
A posted speed limit represents the maximum for ideal conditions, rather than a safe speed for every situation.
On a one-way street, travel only in the direction indicated by the arrow.
A Wrong Way sign warns that you are traveling against the authorized direction on a street, ramp or freeway.
Do Not Enter bars entry into the roadway section it controls.
A red slash through a red circle identifies the action that a regulatory sign forbids.
A rectangular Do Not Pass sign is placed to the right; the supplementary yellow pennant used by some states is placed to the left.
No Turn on Red prohibits the indicated right turn at the controlled intersection, including when the message is electronic.
A two-way center left-turn lane serves left-turning traffic from either direction and cannot be used to pass.
Yellow warning signs with dark lettering call for additional caution because a hazard lies ahead.
For curve or turn warnings, reduce speed before entering; an advisory speed plaque gives the recommended maximum for that curve or turn.
A lane-reduction warning requires a safe move into the continuing lane.
An added-lane sign means entering traffic receives its own lane without a required merge.
A divided-highway-begins warning indicates opposing traffic will be separated; the corresponding ends warning indicates that separation stops.
Intersection warning signs call attention to traffic that may enter your path.
A circular yellow railroad warning sign means a crossing is ahead; slow enough to be able to stop for a train.
Pedestrian and school warning signs may use either standard yellow or fluorescent yellow-green.
A school-ahead sign identifies an approaching school or marked school crossing; the school-crosswalk sign identifies a crossing used by children.
A bump warning calls for lower speed to avoid losing vehicle control.
A slippery-when-wet sign means reduce speed when the pavement is wet.
Cones, drums, tubes, barricades and vertical panels warn of road work and channel traffic through it.
On a striped barricade or panel, downward-right stripes direct traffic to its right; downward-left stripes direct traffic to its left.
Work-zone arrow panels may direct a lane change during daylight or darkness and may also display a caution pattern.
Construction warning signs generally use black messages on orange backgrounds; electronic work-zone signs may change their messages.
Work-zone flaggers use flags or stop-and-slow paddles to stop, slow or guide traffic; follow their directions.
Green direction signs use white text to identify routes, junctions, destinations and distances.
Blue service signs use white symbols, and the access symbol identifies facilities free of mobility barriers.
White symbols on a brown sign identify a recreational area.
A steady red traffic light requires stopping at the stop line or before the crosswalk and remaining stopped until the signal permits movement and the intersection is clear.
A yellow traffic light warns that green is ending and red is about to begin.
A green light permits movement only when the intersection is clear.
A green arrow permits its indicated movement, even alongside red, but drivers must yield to pedestrians and vehicles already within the intersection.
Treat a flashing red signal as a stop sign and proceed only when pedestrians and vehicles are clear.
A flashing yellow signal allows cautious passage through the intersection.
For a left-turn signal, steady red requires waiting, while steady yellow warns that the arrow is changing to red.
A flashing yellow left arrow permits a cautious left turn after yielding to approaching traffic and pedestrians.
A steady green left arrow gives left-turning traffic the right of way.
A broken yellow centerline on a two-way road may be crossed for passing or a left turn.
With adjacent solid and broken yellow lines, a driver beside the solid line cannot pass but may cross it to turn left.
A double solid yellow centerline prohibits passing in both directions; crossing for a left turn remains permitted.
Stop before the wide white stop line, including when a marked crosswalk lies beyond it.
Crosswalks may use two white boundary lines or longitudinal white markings; keep your vehicle out of the pedestrian crossing.
At a railroad advance warning, reduce speed, look and listen, and prepare to stop.
Before crossing multiple railroad tracks, check every track; another train may approach from the opposite direction after the first clears.
At a passive railway crossing, the driver must recognize the crossing, check for trains and decide whether sufficient clear space exists to cross safely.
If trapped on tracks, leave the vehicle and move away at a forty-five-degree angle toward the approaching train, then report through the posted ENS number and call nine-one-one.
Use the posted railroad emergency notification contact to report obstructions or malfunctioning crossing lights or gates.
Roundabout traffic moves counterclockwise around the central island.
Unless signs or markings direct otherwise, use the left lane for a roundabout left turn, the right lane for a right turn and either lane for through movement.
On the interstate, slower drivers keep right and lane changes require both a signal and a clear destination lane.
Lower speed in deer-warning areas and avoid swerving around an animal, which may cause a worse crash.
Accessible parking requires the proper placard or plate; the diagonal access area beside the space must remain clear.
